subject: residual SDs as a random variable

messages.author: 065110cca96a6373
messages.subject: residual SDs as a random variable
parts:
Dear All,

Apologies if this is an inappropriate question for this list.  I have hierarchical data and am interested in allowing the residual variances to differ between people.  Currently, I have been modeling the person-level residual variances as comming from a gamma, but am open to other approaches.  In general, this seems to be working well enough, but it is often slow, primarily it seems because in the warm-up phase, there are rejected proposals, along the lines of:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter is 0:0, but must be > 0!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

Below is some simulated data and model.  I've used JAGS before but am pretty new to Stan --- am I doing anything remarkably silly in terms of model parameterization?

Thoughts sincerely appreciated,

Joshua

require(rstan)
mlmsim2 <- function(n, k, mu, mu.sigma, sigma.shape, sigma.rate, seed = 5346) {
  set.seed(seed)
  m <- rnorm(k, mu, mu.sigma)
  sigma <- rgamma(k, sigma.shape, sigma.rate)
  y <- rnorm(n * k, mean = rep(m, each = n),
    sd = rep(sigma, each = n))
  y2 <- rnorm(k, sigma/sqrt(sigma.shape/(sigma.rate^2)), sd = 3)
  return(list(Data = data.frame(y = y, y2 = y2,
                     ID1 = 1:(n * k), ID2 = rep(1:k, each = n)),
              n = n, k = k, mu = mu, mu.sigma, sigma.shape, sigma.rate, seed))
}

sim.data <- with(mlmsim2(20, 400, 0, 1, 2, 3, 3268), list(
  'y' = Data$y, 'ID2' = Data$ID2,
   'N' = nrow(Data), 'K' = k))

sim.model <- "
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> K;
  int<lower=0> ID2[N];
  real y[N];
}

parameters {
  real u[K];
  real b0;
  real<lower=0> mu_sigmasq;

  real<lower=0> res_sigmasq[K]; // random standard deviation

  real<lower=0> shape;
  real<lower=0> rate;
}

transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> mu_sigma;
  real<lower=0> res_sigma[K];

  mu_sigma <- sqrt(mu_sigmasq);
  for (j in 1:K) {
    res_sigma[j] <- sqrt(res_sigmasq[j]);
  }
}

model {
  b0 ~ normal(0, 1000);
  mu_sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);

  shape ~ gamma(.0001, .0001);
  rate ~ gamma(.0001, .0001);

  for(j in 1:K) {
    u[j] ~ normal(b0, mu_sigma);
    res_sigma[j] ~ gamma(shape, rate);
  }

  for(i in 1:N) {
    y[i] ~ normal(u[ID2[i]], res_sigma[ID2[i]]);
  }
}
"

sim.res <- stan(model_code = sim.model, data = sim.data, chains = 2)

messages.author: 368f61d9252655a2
messages.subject: Re: residual SDs as a random variable
parts:
I think one problem is with the transformed parameters&change of variables part of the code. As you characterize transformed parameters by a distribution you should also be incrementing the log-posterior by determinant of Jacobian of the transform (see for example p. 157 in Stan manual). But why not directly declare mu_sigma and res_sigma as a parameters and get ride of the whole transform?

Secondly, you could use vectorization and eliminate the first loop. Ie:

u ~ normal(b0, mu_sigma);
res_sigma ~ gamma(shape, rate);

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: residual SDs as a random variable
parts:
Good point. These two need Jacobians:

mu_sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
res_sigma[j] ~ gamma(shape, rate);

In both cases, it's a sqrt(x) transform. But we just tend to use the
parameters directly. It's odd to see mu transformed with a square.
As to transforming sigma, that was popular for BUGS because it used
a precision parameterization (1/sigma^2)
and people often care about the scale (sigma).

- Bob

Dear Herra and Bob,

Thank you very much for the tips.  Yes, the transforms were left over from BUGS and working with precisions instead of scale (plus I ran across one Stan example online doing it).

Dropping the transform and just using sigma's directly seems to be helping some.  Much appreciated!

I am familiar with the concept of vectorizing form R, although I do not quite get yet where all in Stan I can and cannot, so thank you as well for the example code of the pieces I can vectorize.

Under various simulations, the model is running pretty well now after the first couple hundred warmup iterations, which makes me think it is a starting values issue.  My hunch is that it is most likely an issue related to the residual variances, so I am thinking about passing start values based on the raw values (i.e., rather than use a hierarchical model, just have R calculate SDs by ID, and get the shape and rate parameters of the gamma as mean^2 / variance and mean/variance).  I'll post back how things go.

Cheers,

Josh

P.S. I saw in the FAQ that a collection of example models might be being made, happy for this to be included under a CC-BY license.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] residual SDs as a random variable
parts:
I'd suggest building up from fewer variables. For instance,
build the non-hierarchical version that fits a different u
and res_sigma per group, but gives them fixed priors rather
than hierarchical ones. That should give you some feeling for
the scale and variation of u and res_sigma.

Then try to add hierarchical priors for
one variable at a time, making sure everything fits.

For speed, you can vectorize
for (j in 1:K) {

u[j] ~ normal(b0, mu_sigma);
res_sigma[j] ~ gamma(shape, rate);
}
to just

u ~ normal(b0, mu_sigma);
res_sigma ~ gamma(shape, rate);

I'd suggest using (k in 1:K) rather than (j in 1:K) to
keep fewer letters and more connection in the notation.
And we would've named mu_sigma sigma_u, because it's the
scale of u; similarly, I'd have used sigma_y instead of res_sigma.
I also wouldn't use "res_sigmasq" for "random standard deviation"
because if it's squared, it's variance.

The gamma priors are also problematic. I know people did
this in BUGS, but they tend to introduce very tail-heavy and
ill-behaved posteriors (in both Stan and BUGS).
Andrew's written about this quite a bit. We tend to use just
something fairly vague, but still peaked near 1 or 0, like
cauchy(0,5). (It'll automatically be a half-Cauchy because
of the constraint on the sigma to be positive.)

Always keep your priors to where they're reasonable. So
if 1000 isn't a reasonable value for b0, then normal(0,1000)
isn't a reasonable prior. Same for the other terms.

- Bob

On Mar 29, 2014, at 9:09 PM, Joshua Wiley <jwiley...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Herra and Bob,
>
> Thank you very much for the tips. Yes, the transforms were left over from BUGS and working with precisions instead of scale (plus I ran across one Stan example online doing it).
>
> Dropping the transform and just using sigma's directly seems to be helping some. Much appreciated!
>
> I am familiar with the concept of vectorizing form R, although I do not quite get yet where all in Stan I can and cannot, so thank you as well for the example code of the pieces I can vectorize.

We have just begun to vectorize the basic functions. But all
of the univariate densities are vectorized on all of their arguments.
(But so far, it doesn't play nicely with truncation.)

> Under various simulations, the model is running pretty well now after the first couple hundred warmup iterations, which makes me think it is a starting values issue. My hunch is that it is most likely an issue related to the residual variances, so I am thinking about passing start values based on the raw values (i.e., rather than use a hierarchical model, just have R calculate SDs by ID, and get the shape and rate parameters of the gamma as mean^2 / variance and mean/variance).

This can help, but usually if there's a model that takes a few
hundred warmup iterations to converge it's often a problem with
too-broad priors. Stan's very good at exploring broad swaths of
the posterior, whereas BUGS/JAGS will appear to be better behaved
because they won't properly sample from the posterior. You can
diagnose by looking at the widths of posterior intervals or posterior sd.
In that case, tighter priors help control inference.
> I'll post back how things go.
Posting back would be great.

> Cheers,
>
> Josh
>
> P.S. I saw in the FAQ that a collection of example models might be being made, happy for this to be included under a CC-BY license.

Even better. Thanks.

- Bob
